newsitem.title: USA: Fed economist--consumption dip not long-term worry.
newsitem.headline: Fed economist--consumption dip not long-term worry.

text.p: Recent weakness in U.S. consumer spending reflects a temporary pullback from sharp gains early this year and not the start of a long-term trend, said Federal Reserve senior economist Charles Luckett.

While retail sales have fallen for the last three months, gains of 1.6 percent in January and 1.3 percent in February show consumer purchases remain healthy, Luckett told Reuters at a forum on consumer finances.

"The level of spending is still pretty strong," said Luckett. "It's hard to say we know that this latest slowdown or leveling off is the start of a downturn. It may just be a pause and then it gets stronger."

Retail sales dipped 0.3 percent in March, 0.9 percent in April and 0.1 percent in May. But gains in consumer confidence measures, like the 28-year high in the Conference Board's May index, suggest spending will rebound, Luckett noted.

"I would guess that (retail sales are) not signalling a serious, long-term slowdown. A lot of things, such as the so-called consumer confidence measures ... they're showing pretty strong," Luckett said.
While some analysts cite high levels of delinquent consumer loans as a warning of impending consumer troubles, Luckett argued they merely reflect changes in the banking sector.

"That tells us as much about creditor behavior as it does the actual conditions of the consumer sector. Most people in the industry would agree that banks are lending to a broader, on average higher-risk clientele," Luckett said.
"I think that is, in part, one reason that delinquencies are higher," he added.

The American Bankers Association reported Tuesday that credit card delinquencies eased lower in the first quarter to 3.51 percent of outstanding accounts after surging in the fourth quarter of 1996 to 3.72 percent.
Luckett said he does not see consumer debt or delinquencies at excessive levels that might jeopardize future spending.
"That's very hard to say," said Luckett. "I haven't seen a whole lot of evidence that some sort of real danger point has been reached."
